doc.title: Bob Stewart interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 24, 2006

chapter: Tuba in jazz history and technique
title: 'Hambone' and New Orleans funeral tradition
summary: Listening to his tune 'Hambone', Stewart explains its New Orleans funeral-march slow-then-fast structure and amplification.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Jazz funerals: dirges, hot return, second line

blocks.x: Maybe we should just listen to the beginning of it. Because it caught my eye right away, that title for one thing and then the groove of this song which I think is very cool.

This is Idris Muhammad playing drums. No I’m sorry, this is not Idris, he’s on a previous album, this is Buddy Williams playing drums but he has an understanding about that New Orleans — he sees where he’s coming from playing. That whole marching band snare drum.
I can just see it going down the street. I mean I’ve only been to New Orleans once but I heard it.

Right. But then the other part of the song is coming from a whole other place. It’s not really coming, ‘cause the reason I’m doing this very slow through the first time, is also coming out of the New Orleans tradition where you’re going to the cemetery playing very slow and when you come back from the cemetery you’re playing happy and hot you know. The second time through the song it gets faster. And that’s again playing homage to the whole tradition of New Orleans while necessarily the music is not traditional but it’s in the tradition.
In the tradition. And then you go to this treatment. Is this a little bit of Con Edison in there with your sound?
Not necessarily with the sound although I am playing through an amplifier, in most of these records I’m playing through an amplifier, because I couldn’t keep this up.
No I thought I heard, did you have an electronic treatment on the sound?
No, not on this song, no. I don’t think I have that treatment on any of these on this particular album.
Maybe it’s just that you’re playing more sustained as opposed to oomph-oomph-oomph.
Well it’s a very catchy, enjoyable album.
